en: My liver crushed and burning,
I had no mortal to help me.
Sobbing bitterly, travelling by night,
My son Bakai, I set out toward Bukhara,
Toward the ancient city of Bukhara.
My son Bakai, ruined, fleeing, wandering on foot,
Your friend's wife who has fled—
Kanykei bears no blame.
To soothe one's longing fully,
To fall into sound sleep,
There is no shelter where we can lie in peace,
No hollow in which to hide.
Your child left by your friend,
To give him even a little to eat,
There is no food or sustenance to keep us alive.
My days have shrivelled miserably.
Unable to reach a known place,
My back has grown bent,
My eyes have grown staring.
Only a spoonful of blood remains;
My flesh is utterly wasted.
Tears fill my eye sockets,
Pain fills my whole breast.
My joints have failed, my strength has gone;
My vigor ebbs, my senses swoon.
Black night has fallen over me.
I fear my orphan will die of hunger;
I fear his death will come today!
Leopard Bakai, my foal,
I have scattered—gather me up.
I have broken—join me together.
Kindle my extinguished fire;
Bring my dead soul back to life!
I am thirsty—quench my thirst.
I am weary—give my soul rest!
Do not press against my throat.
Khan Bakai, guard him as a father!
Nourish this wasted soul;
Fill this hungry belly.
Only son of the saintly old man,
I am thirsty—quench my thirst.
Give me six swift horses.
If you truly honor the departed spirit,
Khan Bakai, give me six skins of milk.
I have set out on a distant journey:
Give the only child a horse to ride away.
Khan Bakai, give a prayer against burning, give your aid.
Give a coat so we will not freeze to death.
So that our bellies will not hunger,
Give plenty of travel rations.
I have no strength to rely upon;
These words are addressed to you alone.
Give my soul a little rest.
“My renowned mother is fierce,” you say.
Fleeing Ken-Kol, running on foot,
I wept in grief and travelled by night.
Unable to reach a known place,
Khan Bakai, utterly helpless, I lay still.
The spring that flows from the hills—
May Allah Most High look kindly upon it.
Will he save this one,
The lamp the Magnanimous left behind!”
Draining Bakai's strength,
Your mother told him
Everything that had happened:
The humiliation Abyke inflicted,
The violence of Kobosh the slave,
The forty swine whom Manas left,
All forty, dog-swine from forty places,
How they plundered her possessions,
How thoroughly they wrought havoc.
When your mother had told him, sobbing,
When the tangled tale's knot
She had unravelled completely,
When the strife with which it began
She had recounted in full,
Your uncle Bakai, the precious khan—
Allah's sun clouded over in the sky;
Sixty cares came into his head.
His ribs seemed to part and split.
His precious eyes, like a saker falcon's,
Shed tears whenever he blinked.
Bakai dissolved in sobbing.
The bloody tears flowing from the noble hero's eyes
Poured down his beard.
His knees bent to the earth;
He despaired of Talas's six villains.
The poor man, lost in many thoughts,
Pressed to his breast and embraced
Semetey, whom Manas left behind.
That child, solid as a tombstone,
He spread across his palms.
Saying, ‘The orphan the Magnanimous left,’
As though Khan Bakai were dividing an inheritance,
He weighed him in his hands,
Holding him up, big and broad:
“You are not yet six months old.
My orphan, are you the one to flee to Bukhara?
Parted from his support,
Am I the Bakai who must wail?
If it appeared by unseen favor,
Did you find a brown wether and eat?
Bakai, who has grown old—
My orphan, let me be your sacrifice—
Did you mean him to suffer your hell?
When I turn to look behind,
Was it a night when Khizyr did not walk?
Parted from you, my orphan,
Was this a day to die in such distress?
My orphan, you have fled away to Bukhara.
Growing to maturity, becoming a man,
Equal to the sons of heroes,
When will you come to Talas?
Before your grieving uncle Bakai's
Eyes, appearing safe and sound,
My soft little mottled-gray falcon,
Semetey, mottled-gray falcon, my morning star,
My spring that flows from the river valley,
Semetey, whom my friend left behind,
My lamp, found at the brink of death!
In the valley of broad Talas
I shall turn my steed's head.
For the offspring the falcon left,
Until twelve years have passed,
I shall keep watch over the camels.
Broad Talas shall be no home for me;
I shall have no peace with the six villains.
If I can, from those six villains,
For your sake, my orphan,
I shall plunder their possessions;
I shall wreak thorough havoc.
Slaying men and cutting off heads,
Clashing many spears,
For your sake, my mother,
On your account, Kanykei,
I myself against the six villains
Shall wage war for twelve years!
Slaying men and cutting off heads,
I shall raise many a tumult.
Taking no rest by day,
Taking no sleep at night,
That is how I shall fight.
Raiding horses, slitting mares,
That is how I shall bring destruction.
Until twelve years have passed,
Keeping them from this Talas,
That is how I shall torment them.
If my means suffice, the villains
I shall isolate and destroy.
Whenever I meet them, every one
I shall offer in sacrifice.
Somehow, against those villains,
I shall avenge my unforgotten grievance!”
Then old Bakai,
Coughing with deep, repeated thuds,
Held Semetey, whose cradle was a leg,
Pressed against his breast.
The wide world grew narrow.
His unfortunate daughter-in-law Kanykei
He now longed to see.
Holding Semetey, distraught,
Pleading with Kanykei,
Mighty Bakai approached.
Though Khan Bakai stood pleading,
Kanykei would not look.
The reason she would not look—
About her great dark head,
Her bloody face was torn.
Her precious hair, like meadow grass,
Lay neatly spread before her.
With her dark head bowed,
She had lost her beloved
At thirty-two years of age.
Without looking upon Bakai's face,
She turned away and screamed,
Falling face down,
Her voice reaching God.
At the sight of Kanykei,
Dignified Khan Bakai wept;
He could not rally himself and watch.
And that gracious old lady Chyiyrdy,
Your mother, wept again.
Then Bakai's voice rang out;
In a deep voice he spoke encouragement:
“Oh, Kanykei, my foal,
Do not be ashamed, my incomparable child.
He who gave his hand to twelve saints,
Saintly Manas, is not here.
You have no support to rely upon.
Do not keep grieving so, Kanykei.
Never giving up their greed,
Never sated by what they beg to eat,
Your sovereign Kyrgyz people are not here.
Wandering the wilderness and wailing,
My child Kanykei, there is no use in endless tears.
May those six restless villains
Not pick up your trail
And chase you to exhaustion.
May the forty companions Manas left
Not pick up your wretched trail
And hunt you until you pale.
May they not trample us down,
Oh, Kanykei, my foal,
Nor scatter blood across the wilderness.
May they not ignore your pleading,
Gouge out your eyes while you live, my child,
And inflict such torment.
May they not snatch the orphan
The Magnanimous left from your hands,
Making a spectacle upon the road,
My child Kanykei, nor tear him open for the vultures!”
Having said these words,
“Oh, Kanykei, my foal,
If you mean to flee, move;
If you mean to leave, fly!
This wilderness is no place for us;
It is not right for us to stay here.
Let us go up into the hills;
If death comes, let us die.
If the six villains inflict humiliation,
We shall face that afterward.”
The saint, a wolf against the enemy,
Your tiger, old Bakai,
Knew this very moment
The torment of six months ahead.
He was a man of sacred power,
A khan over many lands,
Finding words in sudden crisis,
Finding sight in the dark.
His eyes glittered like a lion's.
When he fought his way to Beijing,
He bore the banner of Islam.
His wrath took lives;
His grip drew blood.
Where he went, lives were lost.
Wearing a gray lynx-fur cap,
While his fierce wolf lived,
He wielded a mottled-blue shield.
When he travelled in the dark,
He prowled like a leopard.
Ninety-five counsels, a thousand prayers—
He pondered every one.
Of thoughts in his clear mind,
He left not one untouched.
Hardened by drinking blood,
He was called Leopard Bakai.
Girding his waist securely,
If seventy thousand troops came,
He plunged in lightly clad and attacked.
Your forefather, like a prophet,
Was that same uncle Bakai.
Who defeated enemies in many lands?
Was it not renowned Bakai?
When dark days brought trouble,
While Khan Manas lived,
Who found so many counsels for him?
